name: Engine design: time-stepped vs event-driven, integration scheme, neighbour search at Indian densities, seeded determinism, worker/typed-array architecture, one engine for lane-based and lane-free movement
maintainer: N/A for the decision itself. Evidence from: Eclipse SUMO (DLR) step/integration docs, Treiber and Kanagaraj (integration schemes for car-following models), A/B Street (discrete-event simulator, Dustin Carlino), traffic-simulation.de (Treiber/Kesting), MDN (Web Workers, SharedArrayBuffer), Glenn Fiedler (Fix Your Timestep), PRNG references (bryc/code, Vigna and Blackman xoshiro)
first_release: N/A (design decision). Reference points: Fix Your Timestep article 2004 [uncertain]; Treiber and Kanagaraj integration-scheme comparison 2015 (arXiv 1403.4881, 2014 preprint); A/B Street discrete-event design about 2019-2020 [uncertain]
last_activity: Evidence checked 2026-11-11 (SUMO Basic Definition docs, MDN SharedArrayBuffer page, A/B Street discrete-event doc, 2025 IDM review arXiv 2506.05909)
licence: N/A (our code). Reference PRNG algorithms (mulberry32, sfc32, xoshiro128**) are public domain or permissively published [uncertain per implementation]
language: TypeScript in a Web Worker (same module runnable in Node for headless tests); optional Rust/AssemblyScript to WASM for the hot loop only if profiling demands
code_availability: N/A (design). References: SUMO docs; A/B Street sim crate (github.com/a-b-street/abstreet); traffic-simulation.de JS (github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de); PRNG reference code at github.com/bryc/code/blob/master/jshash/PRNGs.md
maintenance_health: N/A (design decision). The pieces relied on (Web Workers, transferable ArrayBuffers, typed arrays) are stable web platform features; SharedArrayBuffer additionally requires cross-origin isolation headers
network_import: Engine consumes a pre-built link-and-connector JSON (links with polyline, width, level, speed limit, strip count = floor(width / 0.5 m); nodes with connectors, conflict points, signal programs). OSM import (osm2streets-js or a custom Overpass parser) is a separate preprocessing module so the engine never touches OSM; this keeps the engine deterministic and testable
demand_input_formats: OD flows per vehicle class and time slice (veh/h), converted to departures by a seeded Poisson/exponential headway generator from a dedicated PRNG stream; optional explicit trip list for replay. Routes resolved once at insertion (shortest path on the link graph) so routing does not perturb the random stream
runs_in_browser_or_server: Browser: simulation in a dedicated Web Worker, rendering on the main thread (Canvas2D or WebGL). The same TypeScript engine runs in Node for unit tests, golden-run regression tests and any batch runs
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: Pure TypeScript is sufficient for the target load; WASM is an optimisation, not a requirement. Evidence is mixed: an emulator benchmark found the best WASM case only about 2x faster than the slowest JS, while an anecdotal Bevy sprite test showed far larger gaps in both directions, so measure before porting [uncertain]. No streaming from a server is needed; deterministic seeds make results reproducible client-side
api: Engine as a pure module: createSim(network, scenario, seed) -> sim; sim.step(dt) advances one fixed step; sim.snapshot() fills typed arrays (id, x, y, heading, class, level) for rendering; sim.metrics() returns aggregates; sim.apply(edit) for scenario edits between runs. Worker protocol: main thread sends {cmd: start/pause/speed/edit}; worker posts frames as transferable ArrayBuffers (ping-pong two buffers to avoid allocation) at render rate, and metrics at 1 Hz
performance: No published vehicle-count benchmarks exist for browser traffic engines [uncertain]. traffic-simulation.de typically runs hundreds of vehicles at about 30 fps and states decision-making cost is negligible even on smartphones, with graphics dominating (README_3d) [uncertain]. A/B Street's discrete-event docs give no current numbers and identify repeated turn-start attempts and queue checks as the cost centres. SUMO reference (server): the Bologna scenario of about 9,000 vehicles and 5,000 steps takes about 8 s without TraCI. Budget estimate for our engine [uncertain, to be measured]: a 3 km x 2-direction corridor network at 900 veh/km holds about 5,000 vehicles; at dt = 0.2 s and 10x real time that is 250,000 vehicle-updates per second, each needing about 10-30 neighbour checks with a link-local index, which is within reach of optimised JS on typed arrays; rendering 5,000 vehicles needs WebGL instancing or batched Canvas2D paths rather than per-vehicle drawImage calls
gpu_requirement: None for simulation; WebGL optional for rendering
multi_tenancy_model: Fully client-side: each user's browser runs its own scenario, so hosting is static files (zero marginal compute cost per user). Scenario sharing via URL-encoded or stored JSON plus seed reproduces identical results
build_complexity: Low: Vite + TypeScript with module workers (new Worker(new URL('./sim.worker.ts', import.meta.url), {type: 'module'})). SharedArrayBuffer would require COOP: same-origin and COEP: require-corp headers on the host, which also restrict loading third-party resources; transferable ArrayBuffers avoid that requirement and are recommended for a 72-hour build
scenario_editability: Edits (lanes/widths, signals, demand, vehicle mix, flyover templates) are applied while paused and trigger a rebuild of derived structures (strips, conflict points, signal tables); then the run restarts from t = 0 with the same seed, so before/after comparisons differ only by the edit
output_metrics_supported: Determinism enables paired comparisons: travel time and delay per OD and per link, queue length per approach (max and mean), throughput per node, stops, density and speed per link, level of service from delay; dynamic PCU possible from headway or area occupancy. Collected in the worker into fixed-size typed-array accumulators
emissions_support: Not part of the core design; could add per-class speed-acceleration emission factors later
known_limitations: 1) Time-stepped vs event-driven: A/B Street moved to discrete events because most agents are in steady state and per-step acceleration under constraints was complex and error-prone, but its design has instant speed changes, no mid-road lane changes for a long time, and costs that rise when many vehicles queue; this does not suit dense lane-free Indian traffic where every vehicle interacts laterally every step, so a fixed time step is the right choice. 2) Integration: SUMO defaults to a 1 s step with Euler update (speed constant in the step); ballistic update (acceleration constant, position by average speed) is more realistic at larger steps but SUMO notes it works poorly with the sublane model; an action-step-length different from step length forces ballistic; steps larger than the reaction time risk collisions. Treiber and Kanagaraj found the ballistic scheme best for practical purposes among Euler, ballistic, Heun and RK4; for IDM any update step below about 0.5 s gives essentially the same result; ballistic needs a stopping rule to avoid negative speeds. 3) JS floating point is IEEE double and deterministic for + - * /, but Math.sin/cos/exp/pow are implementation-approximated in the ECMAScript spec, so bit-identical results across browsers are not guaranteed if those are used in the update [uncertain about practical impact]. 4) Math.random cannot be seeded. 5) SharedArrayBuffer needs a secure, cross-origin-isolated context
documented_failures: A/B Street: time-step version abandoned because of floating-point edge cases in computing per-step accelerations; discrete-event version has laggy-head checks retried every 0.1 s and turn-start retries as hot spots. SUMO: users get collisions or unrealistic behaviour when action step exceeds the reaction time tau; ballistic plus sublane combination problematic (SUMO issue 2581). Renderer-coupled loops (variable dt from requestAnimationFrame) change simulation results with frame rate and cause a 'spiral of death' under load, which the fixed-timestep accumulator with a clamp (e.g. 0.25 s max frame time) avoids
validation_approach: Golden-run tests: run fixed scenarios headlessly in Node with a fixed seed and compare a hash of the final state and metrics against stored values on every change. Convergence test: halve dt (0.2 -> 0.1 s) and check that link travel times change by less than a few percent. Invariant checks each step in debug builds: no negative speeds, no overlap of vehicle footprints within a link, vehicles conserved (inserted = exited + present). Performance test: steps per second at 1k/5k/10k vehicles in a worker
takeaway_for_our_build: 1) Fixed time step dt = 0.2 s (0.1 s if strip lateral moves look jumpy), ballistic position update with an explicit stop clamp (if v + a*dt < 0, stop at the point where v = 0), same dt for longitudinal and strip-lateral moves; this keeps IDM below the 0.5 s accuracy threshold and avoids SUMO's sublane-ballistic issue by owning the lateral logic. 2) Neighbour search: per-link arrays of vehicle indices sorted by longitudinal position s (re-sorted by insertion sort each step, near O(n) because order barely changes), with each vehicle also storing its strip span [lo, hi]; leader/follower search scans forward/backward in the sorted array until the lookahead distance and keeps only vehicles whose strip spans overlap the candidate strips. At 900 veh/km and 50 m lookahead this is about 45 candidates per scan, so add per-strip-group buckets if profiling shows it hot. Connectors through junctions use the same structure plus conflict-point reservations. Never use a world-space grid: flyovers overlap the road beneath (B07). 3) Lane-based and lane-free in one engine: a lane is just a fixed strip span of width 3.5 m / 0.5 m = 7 strips with lateral moves only allowed as whole-lane changes; lane-free classes may occupy any contiguous strip span; the same sorted-array index serves both. 4) Determinism: seeded sfc32 or xoshiro128** PRNG, separate streams for demand, driver-parameter sampling and behaviour noise (so changing signal timing does not reshuffle arrivals); fixed update order (by link id then position); no Math.random, Date.now, or iteration over Maps/Sets keyed by objects in the update; avoid transcendental functions in the update loop or confine them to precomputed geometry. 5) Two-phase update: compute all accelerations and lateral decisions from the state at t, then apply, so results do not depend on iteration order. 6) Worker architecture: structure-of-arrays Float32Array/Float64Array state in the worker, transferable ArrayBuffer frames to the main thread (ping-pong), renderer interpolates between the last two frames with alpha from the accumulator; skip SharedArrayBuffer to avoid COOP/COEP hosting constraints. 7) Main loop: accumulator with clamp; speed multiplier = number of fixed steps per render frame
